body.heading: Words have beats
paragraphs: Say the word 'rabbit' slowly: rab-bit. Did you hear two beats? Those beats are called syllables. Every word has at least one, and clapping them is the easiest way to count them.
Put your hand under your chin and say a word — your chin drops once for every syllable. Try it with your own name!

body.heading: Two-beat words
paragraphs: rabbit — rab-bit (2). turtle — tur-tle (2). pencil — pen-cil (2). garden — gar-den (2).
Clap once for each beat: clap-clap!

body.heading: Three-beat words
paragraphs: butterfly — but-ter-fly (3). banana — ba-na-na (3). elephant — el-e-phant (3). umbrella — um-brel-la (3).
Tomato — to-ma-to (3). Kangaroo — kan-ga-roo (3). Dinosaur — di-no-saur (3).
Clap-clap-clap for every one of these!

body.heading: One-beat words
paragraphs: Short words often have just one beat. One clap!

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Clap the syllables in everyone's name at dinner tonight. Whose name has the most beats?
2. Find a four-beat word. (Hint: think about a long, stripy, orange vegetable friend… no — think 'hippopotamus' — that's five!)

takeaway: A syllable is a beat in a word — clap or feel your chin drop to count them: rabbit has 2, butterfly has 3, cat has 1.
materials: Just you and this page — no materials needed
supervision: A grown-up nearby is recommended for younger readers; the think-and-talk questions work well read aloud together.
safetyNotes: Reading only — no physical activity or materials are involved.
screenFreeExtension: Clap-and-count walk: name things you pass and clap their syllables — tree (1), flower (2), butterfly (3).
